strengths: Principled and unified formulation: The proposed Priority-Aware Shapley Value (PASV) successfully bridges two previously distinct directions—hard precedence constraints on general DAGs (PSV) and soft individual priority weights (WSV, which was historically constrained to ordered partitions). The inclusion of the |max(S_t)| normalization term is mathematically neat and ensures exact reduction to PSV when weights are equal.

Solid axiomatic foundation: The paper presents an axiomatic characterization for Precedence Random Order Values (PROVs) and shows that within the State-Choice Factorization (SCF) family, natural boundary axioms (Weight Proportionality and Equal-Weight Uniformity) uniquely single out PASV.

Insightful theoretical analysis of limiting regimes: The investigation of extreme priority weights (lambda -> infinity and lambda -> 0+) clearly illuminates how soft priorities interact with the hard precedence graph, accompanied by clear formal results and an informative counterexample showing when extreme weights do not correspond to fixed DAG edge additions.

Efficient local MCMC transition: Lemma 4.1 demonstrates that the adjacent-swap Metropolis–Hastings acceptance ratio simplifies to local neighborhood evaluation at the swapped indices, avoiding costly full-permutation recalculations.

Actionable priority sweeping tool: Beyond point valuation, the priority sweeping framework provides a practically useful sensitivity and stability diagnostic for both data valuation and feature attribution tasks.
weaknesses: Theoretical proofs omitted from appendix: While the main text states key theoretical results (Theorem 3.8, Theorem 3.12, Propositions 3.13 and 3.14, and Lemma 4.1), the manuscript's appendix focuses primarily on experimental setups and does not include formal step-by-step proofs of these core assertions.

Mixing time and scalability analysis of the MCMC sampler: Although Lemma 4.1 makes single-step acceptance ratios efficient to compute, adjacent-swap chains on general posets can suffer from slow mixing times. The paper requires a very large burn-in (100,000) and thinning (10,000) for n=800; a deeper discussion or empirical benchmark on mixing efficiency and wall-clock scaling with respect to player count n is missing.

Heuristic LLM-derived DAG for feature attribution: The general DAG used for the Census Income experiments was constructed by prompting an LLM (ChatGPT). While the authors include the full prompt for transparency, evaluating attribution quality against an ad-hoc LLM-generated DAG provides less rigorous validation than using a validated ground-truth causal DAG or synthetic data with known ground-truth mechanisms.

Absence of empirical comparisons with recent replication-robust baselines: The introduction cites several recent works addressing copier/replication attacks and group structures (e.g., Han et al., 2022; Falconer et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025), but the experimental evaluation compares only against standard SV, WSV, and PSV.

strengths: Unification of precedence constraints and soft priority: The paper successfully bridges the gap between Precedence Shapley Value (which handles general DAGs but assumes uniform weighting over linear extensions) and Weighted Shapley Value (which handles player weights but is restricted to ordered partitions). The inclusion of the $|\max_\prec(S_t)|$ factor in Equation (4) elegantly ensures exact reduction to both PSV and WSV in their respective boundary cases.

Solid axiomatic foundation: The proposed State-Choice Factorization (SCF) along with the natural boundary axioms (Weight Proportionality and Equal-Weight Uniformity) provides a coherent theoretical characterization of PASV.

Analysis of limiting regimes: The investigation of extreme priority weights ($\lambda_i \to \infty$ and $\lambda_i \to 0^+$) gives clear mathematical insight into when soft weights act as additional DAG edges and when they diverge from static edge addition (e.g., the instructive counterexample in Figure 3).

Practical utility of priority sweeping: The 'priority sweeping' diagnostic provides a valuable sensitivity and robustness analysis framework for practitioners to evaluate how context dependence and unreliability/risk affect individual or provider-level payoffs.

Scalable MCMC formulation: Developing the adjacent-swap Metropolis–Hastings sampler for non-uniform linear extension distributions with local acceptance ratio evaluations (Lemma 4.1) makes sampling feasible without recomputing full chain products at each step.
weaknesses: Omission of formal proofs in the appendix: While the propositions and theorems are stated clearly and some are intuitive (e.g., the cancellation of $|\max_\prec(S_t)|$ across permutations in ordered partitions), formal proofs for Theorem 3.8, Theorem 3.12, Proposition 3.13, Proposition 3.14, and Lemma 4.1 are missing from the submitted supplementary material.

Evaluation on downstream data valuation tasks: The data valuation experiments primarily inspect provider-level value distributions, marginal contribution curves, and priority sweep behavior. Standard data valuation benchmarks (e.g., noisy label detection accuracy, point removal curves such as high-to-low and low-to-high accuracy degradation) would provide more quantitative validation of valuation quality against baselines.

Heuristic DAG construction for feature attribution: For the Census Income dataset, the general DAG was constructed via prompting an LLM (ChatGPT-5.2 Thinking). While the authors include the full prompt transcript for transparency, relying on LLM-generated DAG structures introduces potential subjectivity or domain inaccuracies unless accompanied by sensitivity checks against alternative DAG structures.

MCMC mixing and computational overhead: In the experimental setup, sampling linear extensions requires significant MCMC iterations (burn-in of 100,000 and thinning of 10,000 for $n=800$). The manuscript lacks a discussion or empirical analysis of MCMC convergence diagnostics, mixing times, and wall-clock running time comparisons.

strengths: Elegantly bridges two historically separate branches of cooperative game theory: the Precedence Shapley Value (Faigle & Kern, 1992) for posets and the Weighted Shapley Value (Kalai & Samet, 1987) for ordered partitions, unifying them into a single random-order framework (PASV).

Provides an axiomatic foundation through the State-Choice Factorization (SCF) along with Weight Proportionality and Equal-Weight Uniformity, ensuring that PASV reduces precisely to PSV under uniform weights and to WSV on ordered partitions.

Derives an efficient adjacent-swap Metropolis-Hastings acceptance ratio (Lemma 4.1) that depends only on local sets Mk and M'k, avoiding an O(n) re-evaluation of the permutation probability at each proposal.

Offers valuable theoretical and practical insights into the limiting regimes (lambda -> infinity / 0), connecting weight shifts to topological graph modifications and introducing 'priority sweeping' as a diagnostic tool for attribution sensitivity.

Experiments on data valuation (MNIST, CIFAR-10) and feature attribution (Adult Census) are well-analyzed, offering intuitive explanations (e.g., coalition context size and redundancy vs. complementarity) for non-monotone behaviors.
weaknesses: The manuscript states several key theoretical results (Theorem 3.8, Theorem 3.12, Propositions 3.13 and 3.14, Lemma 4.1) but does not include formal mathematical proofs in the main text or the appendix, making full technical verification difficult.

Practical deployment heavily depends on having an accurate precedence DAG and weight specifications; generating the feature attribution DAG via an LLM prompt (Section B.2.3) highlights the sensitivity to subjective or noisy graph constructions.

The data valuation evaluation relies on a k-NN proxy classifier on fixed representations with synthetic providers (copier, poisoner, generators); demonstrating downstream utility on standard data valuation benchmarks (e.g., mislabeled data detection curves, point addition/removal performance on deep networks) would substantially strengthen the empirical claims.

MCMC convergence and mixing rates for adjacent-swap chains on general posets under non-uniform weights are not analyzed; the experimental setup requires large burn-in (B = 100,000) and thinning (tau = 10,000), which may become computationally demanding on larger graphs.

strengths: Principled and unified theoretical formulation: The proposed Priority-Aware Shapley Value (PASV) elegantly unifies hard precedence constraints (general posets/DAGs) and soft priority weights, properly reducing to both the Precedence Shapley Value (PSV) under uniform weights and the Weighted Shapley Value (WSV) under ordered partitions.

Rigorous axiomatization and limit analysis: The paper establishes clear axiomatic foundations (Theorems 3.8 and 3.12) via a state-choice factorization framework, and thoroughly characterizes the limiting regimes as weights approach infinity or zero (Propositions 3.13 and 3.14), complete with illustrative examples and counterexamples.

Tractable computational algorithm: The adaptation of the adjacent-swap Metropolis–Hastings sampler to the non-uniform PASV distribution is backed by Lemma 4.1, which demonstrates that the acceptance ratio can be evaluated using only local information rather than computing global permutation products.

Actionable diagnostics: The proposed 'priority sweeping' and DAG sensitivity analyses turn the potential subjectivity of hyperparameter selection (weights and graph structure) into a practical diagnostic tool for detecting fragile attributions.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Experiments span controlled synthetic benchmarks (testing MCMC mixing time and Monte Carlo convergence against closed-form values up to thousands of players), realistic data valuation scenarios (MNIST and CIFAR-10 with data lineage, generative models, copycats, and poisoners), and feature attribution on Census Income.
weaknesses: Heuristic specification of priority weights: Although priority sweeping offers a useful sensitivity diagnostic, the framework does not provide an automated or data-driven principle for selecting baseline weights $\lambda$, leaving practitioners to rely on domain-specific heuristics.

Dependence on DAG fidelity in feature attribution: In many real-world feature attribution settings, the true underlying DAG is unknown or debatable. While the authors evaluate DAG misspecification and use LLM consultation for the Census DAG, establishing defensible precedence constraints remains a practical challenge.

Worst-case MCMC mixing: While empirical mixing on the tested synthetic graph families scales around $O(n^2)$, adjacent-swap Markov chains on general partially ordered sets can exhibit torpid mixing in pathological or highly constrained poset structures.

strengths: Principled and unified framework: The paper successfully unifies two traditionally separate branches of cooperative game theory—precedence-constrained Shapley values (PSV) and weighted Shapley values (WSV)—into a coherent random-order value framework (PASV) that works on general DAGs and arbitrary positive player weights.

Rigorous theoretical development: The authors provide an elegant axiomatic characterization (Theorems 3.8 and 3.12) based on natural axioms (PROV + SCF + WP + EWU) and clearly analyze the limiting behavior as weights approach infinity or zero, providing clear insights into when soft priority behaves like adding hard DAG edges.

Efficient and scalable algorithm: By establishing Lemma 4.1, the paper shows that the adjacent-swap Metropolis–Hastings sampler's acceptance ratio can be evaluated locally without recalculating the full n-step product, enabling scalable Monte Carlo sampling over linear extensions up to thousands of players.

Extensive empirical and diagnostic evaluation: The experiments cover both practical data valuation (MNIST and CIFAR-10 with realistic data lineage, generative models, copiers, and poisoners) and feature attribution (Census Income), complemented by thorough sensitivity analyses (priority sweeping and DAG edge perturbation studies) and controlled simulation benchmarks.
weaknesses: Axiomatic reliance on the State-Choice Factorization (SCF): Theorem 3.12 relies on the structural assumption that the distribution factors according to the SCF form (Definition 3.9). While motivated by Plackett–Luce multistage models, SCF is a parametric/structural ansatz on the probability distribution rather than a primitive, purely game-theoretic behavioral axiom.

Guidance on calibrating soft priority weights: While 'priority sweeping' is an effective diagnostic for inspecting sensitivity across a range of weights, practical guidance or principled heuristics for choosing baseline numerical values of lambda in complex real-world settings (where trusted priors are incomplete) remains somewhat limited.

Causal DAG validity in feature attribution: The feature attribution DAG in Section 5.2 relies in part on LLM consultation (Appendix F.3). While the sensitivity analysis under DAG misspecification in Section 6.2 and Appendix F.4.2 partially addresses this, attribution conclusions remain sensitive to strong structural assumptions regarding feature precedence.

strengths: Unification of hard precedence constraints (DAGs/posets) and soft priority weights (player-specific weights) into a single coherent random-order value framework, bridging the gap between Precedence Shapley (Faigle & Kern, 1992) and Weighted Shapley (Kalai & Samet, 1987).

Rigorous theoretical grounding, including the axiomatization of Precedence Random Order Values (PROV, Theorem 3.8), the unique characterization of PASV under the State-Choice Factorization (SCF) and natural boundary axioms (Theorem 3.12), and an illuminating analysis of limiting regimes (Propositions 3.13 and 3.14).

Computationally practical MCMC formulation: Lemma 4.1 proves that the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance ratio under adjacent swaps can be computed purely from local information at the swapped indices, avoiding full path re-evaluations and enabling tractable sampling.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across synthetic benchmarks (sum-of-unanimity games up to n=8192), realistic data valuation (MNIST and CIFAR-10 data markets with 800 players and generative/copier/poisoner agents), and feature attribution on tabular data.

The proposed 'priority sweeping' and DAG perturbation analysis provide actionable sensitivity and robustness diagnostic tools for practitioners facing uncertain prior weights or DAG misspecifications.
weaknesses: Specifying both the partial order DAG and the soft priority weights requires domain expertise or heuristics (e.g., using an LLM to propose relations as in Appendix F.3), which can introduce subjective modeling bias into the resulting attributions.

While the adjacent-swap MCMC sampler demonstrates good empirical mixing on the tested synthetic poset families, adjacent transpositions on general posets can theoretically suffer from slow mixing in pathological graph structures (e.g., posets with severe conductance bottlenecks).

The optional quadratic proxy regression estimator (Appendix D.2) scales with O(N_{coef} d^2) where d can be up to O(n^2), leading to steep memory footprints (tens of gigabytes at n=2048) that limit its applicability to moderate player sizes unless carefully regularized.
